Think
thĭngk
v. (to exercise the mind, judge, purpose; rendering Hebrew chashab, zakar, Greek logizomai, phroneo)
From Anglo-Saxon thencan, closely joined to thancian, to thank — thinking and thanking share a root, and Scripture keeps them close.

Biblical Definition

Think in the Authorized Version usually means to reckon or to purpose, not merely to have a passing notion. Joseph asks the butler, “think on me when it shall be well with thee” (Gen 40:14) — remember me, act on it. Nehemiah's repeated prayer is the same word turned Godward: “Think upon me, my God, for good” (Neh 5:19), and against his enemies, “think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works” (Neh 6:14). It also names presumption: Abijah rebukes the northern kingdom — “ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD” (2Ch 13:8) — a plan, not a musing. And Mordecai uses it for the fatal self-deception of the sheltered: “Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews” (Est 4:13). Paul then gives the Christian mind its standing curriculum in Philippians 4:8, ending with the imperative that governs the whole list — think on these things.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines think as to have the mind occupied on some subject, to judge, to conclude, to determine — and to intend or mean, as in he thinks to deceive us.

expand to see more

THINK, v.i. To have the mind occupied on some subject; to have ideas, or to revolve ideas in the mind.

2. To judge; to conclude; to hold as a settled opinion.

3. To intend; to mean.

Let him that thinketh he standeth, take heed lest he fall. 1 Cor. x.

Key Scripture

Php 4:8 — "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things."

Est 4:13 — "Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther, Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews."

Neh 5:19 — "Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people."

2Ch 13:8 — "And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods."

Modern Corruption

The mind treated as a passive receiver of whatever passes through it, and thought as involuntary — where Scripture commands a curriculum and holds a man responsible for what he dwells upon.

expand to see more

The modern assumption is that thoughts happen to a man and only actions are his. Philippians 4:8 is an imperative: think on these things, with an itemized list of what qualifies. That presupposes the mind can be directed — not that stray thoughts can be prevented, but that what a man dwells on is a matter of obedience. In an economy engineered to occupy attention continuously, this command has become both harder and more urgent, and it cannot be obeyed passively.

Esther 4:13 supplies the sharpest warning to the comfortable, and it is the same verb. Mordecai does not tell Esther she is obliged to act because she is powerful; he tells her not to think with herself that the palace will save her. Self-deception is a species of thinking, done privately and plausibly, and it flourishes exactly where a person has enough shelter to make it seem reasonable. The remedy Mordecai offers is not a better feeling but a truer reckoning: deliverance will arise elsewhere, and who knows whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon, devise, impute; zakar (H2142), to remember — the word behind think on me; Greek logizomai (G3049), to reckon, and phroneo (G5426), to set the mind.

expand to see more

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, reckon, devise; the same verb used when righteousness was counted to Abraham (Gen 15:6).

Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; Nehemiah's think upon me, my God is a plea for remembrance, not attention (Neh 5:19).

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, take account of; the imperative in Php 4:8, a bookkeeping word applied to the mind.

Usage

"“Think on these things” — a commanded curriculum for the mind."

"“Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape” — self-deception is a kind of thinking."

"“Think upon me, my God, for good” — a plea for remembrance."
